newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK - Reforms on hold for Sao Joao.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK - Reforms on hold for Sao Joao.

text.p: Brazil's reform program, bogged down for months by political infighting, corruption scandals and disarray in the government's congressional command, faces another delay this week in the form of a revered saint.

Officials in Congress said they expected many lawmakers from Brazil's north and northeast to remain at home for week-long festivities celebrating the June 24 feast day of St John, or Sao Joao as he is known locally.

"There are going to be a lot of absentees this week because Sao Joao really is a big deal," said Giselle Artur, a spokeswoman for deputy Luis Eduardo Magalhaes, the government's chief whip in the Chamber of Deputies.
"For politicians, attending the parties means votes in next year's elections," she said.

Last week, the president of the lower house, Deputy Michel Temer, threatened to fine lawmakers who fail to show up for scheduled votes this week on amendments to the government's civil service reform bill.

Voting on key amendments has been delayed for more than two months after the government failed to muster the three-fifths majorities needed to kill two proposed changes to the bill floated by opposition parties.

But already, most analysts and political columnists believe the government will leave the voting until July, when it is expected to call an extraordinary session of Congress to run through the month-long recess.

Senior whips were reported to be discussing Monday the agenda of a possible extraordinary session, which would include progress on the civil service reform bill and on a pension reform bill currently awaiting a panel-level vote in the Senate.
Other items expected to be dealt with in July include a bill extending the government's Fiscal Stabilization Fund (FEF), which is due to expire June 30.
The fund allows the National Treasury to retain more than $20 billion in receipts earmarked by the constitution for states and municipalities and cover shortfalls in the federal budget.
A bill extending the FEF until 1999 is currently awaiting a first vote in a Chamber of Deputies panel.

In the Senate, the most urgent item on the agenda is a request by the state government of Rio de Janeiro for approval a 3.0 billion real loan which would pave the way for privatization of state bank Banerj.
The Senate's Economic Affairs Committee was due to meet Tuesday to continue discussions on the loan. The full Senate must also approve the deal.

The proposed loan from state mortgage bank Caixa Economica Federal would be used to address Banerj's pension and payroll debts, which currently make the bank unsellable. But senators were irritated by the way Rio de Janeiro submitted its request.
"They left it to the last minute and then failed to include a lot of essential paperwork," said an official close to the negotiations to muster support for the loan.
Rio officials have suggested they might hand Banerj over to the Central Bank for possible liquidation if the Senate does not approve the loan this week.
